questions.question: How does binary search work on a sorted Go slice?
questions.title: How does binary search work on a sorted Go slice
questions.direct_answer: Binary search finds a target in sorted data by comparing the middle element and discarding the half that cannot contain the answer. Its search interval shrinks by roughly half each step. Keep a half-open interval `[low, high)`. If the middle value is below the target, move `low` to `mid+1`; otherwise move `high` to `mid`. The final position is the first value not less than the target.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Binary search finds a target in sorted data by comparing the middle element and discarding the half that cannot contain the answer. Its search interval shrinks by roughly half each step.

Keep a half-open interval `[low, high)`. If the middle value is below the target, move `low` to `mid+1`; otherwise move `high` to `mid`. The final position is the first value not less than the target.

For example, in `[2,4,4,9]`, the predicate `values[i] >= 4` first becomes true at index one. The same index is the insertion point that keeps the slice sorted.

`sort.Search(n, predicate)` can return `n` when no position satisfies the predicate. Always check the index before reading the slice, and define how duplicates should be handled.

Use `sort.Search` when the condition can be written as false for an initial range and true afterward. It encodes the boundary search and avoids repeating index arithmetic.

sections.title: The core model: binary search in Go
sections.content:
binary search in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

The key invariant is that the answer, if it exists, remains inside the current interval. Sorted order tells which side cannot contain it after one comparison. Halving an interval of n elements takes logarithmically many steps, while the algorithm uses constant extra space in its iterative form.

sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Sorted interval low..high] --> B[Check middle]
  B --> C{middle below target?}
  C -- yes --> D[Move low right of middle]
  C -- no --> E[Move high to middle]
  D --> A
  E --> A
```

sections.content:
The useful question is not whether binary search in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: binary search in Go
sections.content:
Failures around binary search in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

If `high` is inclusive in one line and exclusive in another, a one-element interval behaves incorrectly. Another classic error is assigning `low=mid` when mid already failed; the interval may stop shrinking. Half-open bounds with `mid := low+(high-low)/2` give consistent updates.

sections.title: The important trade-off: binary search in Go
sections.content:
binary search in Go and a linear scan solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

Binary search pays off when sorted order already exists or many lookups share the sorting cost. For an unsorted slice and one query, a linear pass is O(n), while sorting then searching is O(n log n). Data updates also matter because maintaining sorted order has a cost.
